In a single payer system, the healthcare provider is being paid not by the patient but by a government entity. Whoever pays the bill is the customer.

I realize that the government is spending money that was provided to it in the form of taxes, but in a single-payer system, the government is the one negotiating with healthcare providers.

Ideally, a free market will drive efficiency. However, when people are in pain, they can't negotiate rationally. They want the pain to stop no matter what the cost. They've also gotten used to ignoring their health and expecting a quick fix via medication or surgery rather than making the lifestyle changes they should have made years ago. When given a terminal diagnosis, many will approve a treatment plan that will extend their life for a few months but has a cost of over $100,000.

I think the best we can likely do is a system that puts the patient in control when it comes to cost. This means that everyone has a high deductible insurance plan so they won't go broke if they are hospitalized and a health savings account to pay for doctor visits, prescriptions, etc. Healthcare providers should be required to provide price lists that are simple and concise, which would lead to price competition that really doesn't exist in healthcare today. There's no reason they can't do this now. This puts the patient in the position of deciding how to spend their money.

Such a system can be socialized in that it's subsidized by the government based on income. If the individual wants to contribute to it to get a better plan, they can do so. What I'm suggesting would be a truly free market plan, which we don't have today because costs aren't generally discussed until after the fact. Most people don't even realize how much they can negotiate down their hospital bills either. However, we do need everyone to be insured because hospitals are required to treat anyone who comes in.

Such a system, in my humble opinion, provides the best of both worlds and is simpler than existing healthcare reforms.

It's not perfect. The healthcare providers still have significant control, but at least published price lists would bring the cost of service front and center where it belongs and hopefully create some downward price pressure as well. We also need to find a way to get doctors out of defensive practice mode, where they order far more tests than necessary just to decrease the likelihood of being sued.

One only needs to accept a couple of simple propositions as morally valid to refute the article's claims and the necessity of religion as a moral guide (as if the historical record of nearly all religions isn't sufficient on its own):

1) We should each expect to be treated as we treat others.

2) We each hold ultimate authority over our own minds and bodies.

If you can accept these two propositions as morally valid, I believe you need nothing more to establish a moral framework.

To be moral is to act rightly when no one is observing. If your actions are driven by fear of punishment from others or a higher power, you are not motivated by a genuine desire to be moral but rather by a wish to avoid suffering. Your belief is functioning as a moral substitute.

If each of our brains was truly random, that would be true. Over millions of years, many animals have evolved to seek protection from a group. Fish, herding animals, pack animals, and humans all seek protection from a group. It could be that the desire to do so was a genetic accident, with those preferring the company of others to solitude being more likely to survive and pass on their genes. That was certainly the case with the domestication of wild canines into companion animals. Those that were comfortable around humans benefited from being able to get scraps and eventually being fed by them.

Over time, this has led us to evolve into beings whose brains see the benefits of group membership. Those that could successfully become members were those that understood there would be rules they approved of and rules they didn't, but that the group as a whole agreed to live within the rules regardless of personal acceptance or rejection. To live outside of them meant being ostracized or even cast out.

Essentially, our brains have evolved to accept that there are rules that the majority has agreed upon and that we each must thus accept. Your output becomes my input and could change my logic. For example, I used to be pro-death penalty until a family member presented me with an excellent argument against it, which changed my mind. They provided the output that became my input and changed my logic. Now my output to others on that topic is different than it was before.

However, where we are headed here is that free will is absolutely an illusion. I can't see how it could be otherwise and be compatible with the natural world. Once you accept that, holding people responsible for their actions makes no sense. However, holding them accountable still absolutely does. If someone is a danger to others, we need to remove them from society (and ideally treat them) until we are convinced they can safely return. Arbitrary sentences make no sense at all, especially when no treatment is provided. That's why we have a high recidivism rate in some regions. Instead, crime should be treated as a mental illness, with offenders required to be treated and not released until we are confident they won't reoffend (are cured). If we don't have the technology to cure them, why would we ever release them? Once we recognize that free will is an illusion, we can begin the process of reinventing our system of justice.

However, there's benefit before even doing that. Once you decide that free will is an illusion, you can recognize that getting angry at someone makes no sense at all. We each make the best decisions we can make at the time we make them with the information we had. If someone doesn't meet your expectations, it was never going to be any different. The best thing to do is figure out how to help them meet your expectations in the future and, of course, hold them accountable to the degree that makes sense.

Rewards and punishments are simply more inputs that we hope will change a person's logic to something closer to our expectations of them.

I went to the government health insurance marketplace and there's now only ONE insurance company providing insurance as far as I can tell. That's a well-known insurance company. The closest thing they have is the same deductible but an HMO so we'd have to switch doctors. The premium however is 56% higher than we are paying now.

Keep in mind these are high deductible plans. If my spouse and two children somehow hit their limits in the same year, we could be out of pocket $20,000 or more.

In looking for another way I came across something called a Health Share plan. I'd never heard of them before but there are several organizations that provide them and they have been around for a couple of decades now. They are all non-profits and I get the feeling they rely on word of mouth to keep their costs down. That explains why I had never heard of them. I mentioned it to a friend in the financial services business and he had. I guess that shouldn't surprise me.

Health Share plans are not insurance but they work the same way. For all practical purposes, they are insurance. You have a monthly premium which they call your Monthly Shared Amount and a deductible called your "Annual Unshared Amount" (at least with the one we are going with). They have a large pool of members (in the hundreds of thousands). Your annual well-check is automatically covered (just like with an ACA plan) but any other visits are paid by you until you reach your Annual Unshared Amount. Basically, your Monthly Shared Amount goes into a pool and is used to pay bills for other members (just like insurance). In fact, they even show you the initials and dollar amount of any members whose bills are paid via money you paid as your Monthly Shared Amount. You can't see who or what it was for but at least you know you helped someone out. It's all completely computerized of course. You can even send the other member a private note if you want to wish them well.

It works pretty much the same as health insurance and it's exempt from the ACA so you won't pay a tax penalty. You get a membership card and when you go to the doctor, hospital, etc. you tell them that you are a self-pay and to send the bill to the address on the card. I'm told that in most cases, they will do that. If they don't, you get the bill, scan it and submit it yourself. As long as the expense is an eligible expense (and it appears that pretty much anything your typical health insurance policy covers is considered eligible), once you have reached your Annual Unshared Amount, the health share plan pays 100% of the rest.

So far it's just like health insurance, right? Here's where it's different. For a single person, the Annual Unshared Amount (which is their term for deductible) is $500. It's $1000 for a couple (which can be a married couple, a parent and child, or two children) and for a family (anything more than two) it's $1500. So for my family, the most we can be out of pocket in a year is $1500 compared to over $20,000 with our former insurance. If I had stuck with our current insurance, our monthly premium would have been $680. With the health share plan it's only $400. So I'm paying a lot less for much better coverage. My company pays $740 per month just to cover me and that's with a $2000 deductible. I could drop that and add myself to our family health share plan for an extra $50 per month. That's a $690 per month savings. They cover some things insurance companies won't cover such as alternative medicine. They cover you when you are out of the country as well. All they ask is that the cost not be more than it would likely be here in the US, that the invoices be in English and in US dollars. If they tell you they aren't going to pay for something, they ENCOURAGE you to call them and work it out. They say that most things can be resolved over the phone. If not, they have two more levels of negotiation you can go through.

If you're single and under 30 years old, the cost for their BEST plan is only $149 per month. That's $1 million in coverage per incident with no lifetime maximum. Because I'm only signing up my spouse and two children, they are giving us the single parent discount saving us $50 per year.

I used to teach programming. I got to watch my predecessor teach each of the two classes once then I had to take over. He taught the parts. Here's what a variable is and how to use it. Here's what an array is and how to use it. Here's what a loop is and how to use it. I followed this same way of teaching for a few years.

Over time, I noticed that after I got a certain way into the class, people's lightbulbs would start coming on. They would start to understand how all these pieces worked together. That's when I had an epiphany of my own. I was teaching absolutely backwards.

The brain stores new information by connecting it to information you already know. Instead of teaching people how the parts worked and then them eventually seeing how all of these parts could be used to solve problems, I started with the problems themselves.

I would introduce a problem that they could all identify with. That allowed them to have a place inside their heads at which to anchor everything I was about to teach them. I would then show them the parts they need to solve that problem. It often meant that I wasn't teaching them everything about variables, arrays or loops, just what they needed to know to solve the problem I had identified at the outset, but that's OK because eventually we'd move on to some other problem that required I teach them more about those same items I had covered earlier.

This might feel like an inefficient approach because I'm going back over items I'd already discussed rather than discussing each one completely before moving on. However, from the perspective of the student, how they learn, and how the brain works, it was the most efficient method of teaching I could imagine. I actually had people coming up to me after class telling me that it was the best class they'd ever taken on any subject. It was simply that I figured out you need to start with something the student already understands and link all the new information to that. They needed to understand why what they were learning was important from the outset rather than afterwards as too many educators do.

I'm not intending to do that. I'm intending to make sure people understand that what works for some individuals won't work for others. All too often we hear about solutions that are broadcast as if they will solve problem X for everyone only to find out that it's not that simple. It would be better to say, if you're having trouble falling asleep, look at what you are doing in the hours preceding that. Are you consuming caffeine? Try not doing that. Are you reading? Are you on your phone? Try avoiding these things one by one and see what impact, if any, that has. Hopefully at some point you will be able to tell which are impacting your sleep and then you'll know what to do to get better sleep.

Your decisions are the result of your neurons and synaptic connections. Those are the result of your immediately prior brain state, which is influenced by your brain state immediately prior to that, all the way back to your early childhood experiences and genetics, neither of which you authored. This means that the idea that you can truly choose between options is an illusion. Your brain will follow a path to a conclusion. Since you can't alter your neurons and synaptic connections, you're not in control of the path your brain takes to a decision. It is your brain that makes the decision, but it does so based on its current physical state. How can there be any free will in that?

What did you have for breakfast this morning? Why did you have it? If you trace that back a few steps, you quickly reach a point where you can no longer answer the why question. If you can't explain why (beyond something like, "When I was a child, a parent made eggs for breakfast, so now I have eggs."), where is the free will in that?

Have you ever noticed how the better you know someone, the more accurately you can predict their behavior? That's because, with experience, you've learned how their mind works. They are just the machine inside of which those processes occur. The ability to predict their behavior indicates that we are each wired a certain way. Where's the free will in that?

When individuals operate far enough outside the bounds of what society deems acceptable, we say they have broken the law. In most cases, this means they have some degree of mental illness. It might be as simple as enjoying the thrill of petty theft, or as serious as engaging in harmful behaviors. In all these cases, they are struggling with mental health issues.

Currently, we impose prison sentences of arbitrary lengths as a form of retribution for their actions. They often emerge from prison in a worse state than when they entered. Instead, we should focus on treating them and then releasing them when we are sufficiently convinced they are no longer a threat. That could be six months or it could be never.

Once you accept that free will is an illusion, you realize that our current criminal justice system is nonsensical and highly inefficient. You should also recognize that getting angry at people for not meeting your expectations is unreasonable. We are all making the best decisions we can at the time, based on the information we have. If someone doesn't meet your expectations, that was the best they could do at that moment.
